newsitem.title: GREECE: OLYMPICS-ATHENS WELCOMES IOC EVALUATION REPORT.
newsitem.headline: OLYMPICS-ATHENS WELCOMES IOC EVALUATION REPORT.

text.p: Greek Olympic officials welcomed on Thursday a positive evaluation by the International Olympic Committee (IOC) on Athens' bid to host the 2004 Games and said a place in the short-list was the next target.
"We are satisfied from the report sent to us by the evaluation commission," the president of Athens' 2004 bidding committee, Yanna Angelopoulos, said in a statement.
"We will now be concentrating our efforts to get on to the short-list."
Another senior Greek Olympic official who did not wish to be named went even further.
"The report was better than we expected and the IOC found things in Athens better than they expected. Rome has a strong bid but we are looking good as well," he said.
Five of the 11 cities vying for the Games will be short-listed on March 7 in Lausanne with the successful venue being announced on September 5.
After the initial appraisals, Athens, birthplace of the Games in 776 BC and venue of the first modern edition in 1896, and Rome were the favourites.
Cape Town, Buenos Aires, Istanbul, Lille, Rio de Janeiro, San Juan, Stockholm, Seville, and St Petersburg are the other cities battling for a place among the five finalists.

The IOC report ignored the security problems which hampered the city's failed bid for the 1996 Games but praised a 96.4 percent local support for the bid, the biggest among the 11 candidates, and high quality facilities with the Olympic Village only 30 minutes from the city.

Pollution remains a problem in Athens but the report commented positively on multi-billion dollar proposals to rid the city of 250,000 cars by building a new airport, new highways and a subway system.
But Greenpeace, the international environmental group, said the report had not paid enough attention to the potential problems.
"The environmental side of the bid file was insufficient," said Greenpeace spokesman, Stelios Psomas.
"We have seen no provisions for the long-term protection of the environment in the planned large-scale construction for the Olympics," he said.
